title: How Latin America Learned to Stop Printing Money
gist: Arturo Porzecanski reviews Luis Jácome's book Central Bank Independence and Inflation, which argues central bank independence with a low-inflation mandate is the most significant economic reform of our time and finds central bank financing of government deficits best explains Latin American inflation.

insights.claim: From the 1960s through the 1990s Latin America was the world's regional outlier in frequency and severity of inflationary, currency, debt and banking crises, but over the past three decades most governments adopted more responsible fiscal and monetary policies with independent, inflation-focused central banks and largely market-determined exchange rates.
insights.speaker: ARTURO C. PORZECANSKI
insights.so_what: Structural improvement in policy frameworks underpins lower tail risk for regional macro assets versus past decades.

insights.claim: Jácome argues that granting central banks political independence while mandating low inflation is arguably the most significant economic reform of our time.
insights.speaker: ARTURO C. PORZECANSKI
insights.so_what: Independence is a core variable to monitor when assessing inflation and currency risk in an emerging market.
insights.quote: is arguably the most significant economic reform of our time.

insights.claim: After the gold standard ended in the mid-1930s and the U.S. dollar standard ended in the early 1970s, most Latin American central banks lost the printing-press discipline those regimes had imposed once currencies could devalue.
insights.speaker: ARTURO C. PORZECANSKI
insights.so_what: Loss of an external anchor historically preceded monetary indiscipline, relevant to any anchor-removal scenario.
insights.locator: He makes his case in two ways

insights.claim: From the 1950s, interventionist policies turned central banks into de facto development banks channeling concessional credit to import-substituting industry and funding government deficits and unprofitable state-owned enterprises, producing excess monetary growth and periodic financial crises.
insights.speaker: ARTURO C. PORZECANSKI
insights.so_what: Monetary financing of fiscal deficits is the key warning sign of coming inflation and crisis.

insights.claim: Jácome builds an index of central bank independence and mission focus back to each bank's founding and finds a statistically significant relationship between better central banking and lower inflation in static and dynamic terms.
insights.speaker: ARTURO C. PORZECANSKI
insights.so_what: Provides econometric support for treating central bank governance as a predictor of inflation.

insights.claim: The main finding is that the extent to which the central bank underwrites government deficits best explains resulting inflation.
insights.speaker: ARTURO C. PORZECANSKI
insights.so_what: Track central bank financing of the treasury as the lead indicator of inflation risk.
insights.quote: the extent of central bank underwriting of government deficits best explains the resulting inflation

insights.claim: Jácome was appointed in September 1998 as first head of a constitutionally independent Banco Central del Ecuador and resigned six months later after President Jamil Mahuad refused to respect its autonomy and took counterproductive measures amid a banking crisis that became a full-blown meltdown.
insights.speaker: ARTURO C. PORZECANSKI
insights.so_what: Legal independence does not guarantee insulation from political pressure; watch executive-central bank conflicts.
insights.locator: Jácome has shared his riveting personal story

insights.claim: Porzecanski notes the book would benefit from accounts of independent central bankers such as Martín Redrado, Arminio Fraga, Julio Velarde and Ruth de Krivoy.
insights.speaker: ARTURO C. PORZECANSKI
insights.so_what: Names regional central bankers associated with independence.
insights.locator: What I wish the thoroughly researched book had included
